title: The Science of Sleep: Why Your Brain Needs Rest

slides.heading: The Science of Sleep
slides.body: Why Your Brain Desperately Needs Rest Every Night

slides.heading: Sleep Is Not Passive
slides.body: While your body rests, your brain is intensely active during sleep. It cycles through distinct stages — NREM and REM — each serving a critical biological purpose. Far from downtime, sleep is one of the most productive states your brain enters.

slides.heading: The 90-Minute Sleep Cycle
slides.body: Sleep moves in ~90-minute cycles, each containing light sleep, deep sleep, and REM stages. Adults need 4–6 full cycles per night. Waking mid-cycle leaves you groggy — a phenomenon called sleep inertia that can last up to 30 minutes.

slides.heading: Memory Consolidation Happens at Night
slides.body: During deep (slow-wave) sleep, the hippocampus replays the day's experiences and transfers them to long-term cortical storage. Skipping sleep after learning something new can erase up to 40% of what you studied, according to research by Matthew Walker at UC Berkeley.

slides.heading: The Brain's Cleaning System
slides.body: During sleep, the glymphatic system flushes toxic waste products — including amyloid-beta plaques linked to Alzheimer's — from the brain. This clearance is up to 60% more effective during sleep than while awake, making quality sleep essential for long-term brain health.

slides.heading: REM Sleep and Emotional Regulation
slides.body: REM (Rapid Eye Movement) sleep acts as overnight emotional therapy. The brain reprocesses difficult memories in a low-stress neurochemical environment, stripping away their emotional charge. Poor REM sleep is strongly linked to anxiety, depression, and PTSD.

slides.heading: Sleep Deprivation's Hidden Costs
slides.body: Just one night of fewer than 6 hours raises cortisol, impairs glucose metabolism, and reduces immune cell activity by 70%. Chronically sleeping under 7 hours is associated with doubled risk of cardiovascular disease, obesity, and cognitive decline.

slides.heading: Circadian Rhythm: Your Internal Clock
slides.body: A master clock in the hypothalamus (the suprachiasmatic nucleus) regulates your 24-hour sleep-wake cycle using light cues. Blue light from screens after sunset suppresses melatonin by up to 3 hours, delaying sleep onset and reducing overall sleep quality.

slides.heading: Evidence-Based Sleep Hygiene
slides.body: Science-backed habits include keeping a consistent wake time (even on weekends), keeping your bedroom below 67°F (19°C), avoiding alcohol within 3 hours of bed (it suppresses REM), and a 20-minute wind-down with dim light before sleep.

slides.heading: Sleep Is a Superpower
slides.body: Every hour of quality sleep is an investment in memory, mood, immunity, and longevity. Prioritize your sleep — your brain is counting on it.
